_readme: The access-control catalogue. This file is the source of truth for who can do what.
Editing it: add a permission to the `permissions` list, then list its `code` under every role
that should hold it. A role granting a permission that is not in the list fails the build, so a
typo cannot silently remove someone's access.
`rank` is the seniority ladder, and it is what stops privilege escalation. Lower is more
senior. Permissions alone cannot express this: in M01 a manager and an owner hold the same
seven permissions, so without rank a manager could promote themselves. Change a number here
to change the ladder.
There are TWO rank rules, and the difference matters:
may_assign_rank  - appointing. Sideways and downward. A manager may appoint another
manager, because lateral appointment is not escalation.
may_reset_password - acting AS someone. STRICTLY more senior, because a password is not
authority over a person, it is the ability to be them: every order, void
and audit row afterwards names the victim. Two owners are the exception,
or a locked-out owner has no recovery path and the product is gone.
Both are judged on the target's most senior role ANYWHERE in the organization, never at the
actor's branch. Roles are per branch; a password, a login and an employment are not. Judging
them per branch let a branch manager take over an admin who covered shifts there (P1-2).
Nobody may change their own roles at all, which closes the last route.
Changes take effect through a migration, not a redeploy of code - the catalogue is seeded into
the `permission`, `role` and `role_permission` tables so that access control is version
controlled and diffable (ADR 0007). Run `make revision` after editing.
Roles with no permissions listed are real roles that simply have nothing to do in M01. They
gain permissions as later modules land (a waiter gets order.create in M07).
`owner` and `admin` hold identical permissions today. They diverge in later modules, where
financial reporting is owner-only.

permissions.description: See the staff list and open an individual employee record.
Add a new employee, optionally with a login.
Change an employee's name, contact details or employment terms.
Deactivate or reactivate an employee. Deactivating ends every open session immediately.
Grant or remove an employee's roles at a restaurant. This is the privilege-escalation path — hold it narrowly.
Set a new password for another employee. Ends all of that person's other sessions.
Read the role and permission catalogue, for the role-assignment screen.
Change the restaurant's settings, floor plan, kitchen stations and tax rates.
Read the menu: categories, dishes, variants and modifiers. A waiter cannot take an order without it.
Create and change categories, dishes, variants and modifiers — everything about the menu except what it costs.
Set a variant's price and its tax group. Separate from menu.manage because it is the money path: seed/organization.yaml withholds it from a manager by name.
Read recipes and their quantities. A chef reads recipes — that is the job.
Create stock items and recipe versions. Held by the chef, who owns the recipe, and the owner.
See what a dish costs and what it earns. Deliberately not the chef's: seed/organization.yaml's design says a chef sees grams, not rupees.
See what is on hand, what is expiring, and the movements behind both. Read-only: it shows the position, it cannot change it.
Record a delivery arriving. Held by the store manager, who takes the delivery, and by the manager and owner above them.
Make a preparation batch, consuming its inputs. The chef holds this and not stock.receive: a kitchen turns ingredients into gravy, it does not sign for the sack.
Post a correction to the ledger. The one movement nobody observed, which makes it the one an insider would use to erase a shortfall — so it always carries a reason and always writes an audit row.
See the supplier list, purchase orders, goods receipts and the supplier variance report. Read-only, and commercially sensitive: it is who you buy from and what you pay.
Add or change a supplier. Not held by the kitchen: inventing a supplier is how purchases get laundered, so create and edit are audited with the actor and a supplier is deactivated, never deleted.

Raise, send and cancel purchase orders. Separate from stock.receive on purpose - posting a delivery writes the stock ledger, so it is the ledger's permission, and the accountant who reconciles invoices can raise an order without ever signing for one.

Open a count sheet, record what is on the shelf, and approve the result. Approval is what posts the corrections, and the service refuses an approver who is also the counter — a control carried by a CHECK constraint as well, so it holds for a path that forgets to ask.
See orders, bills, invoices and credit notes. The accountant holds this and nothing else on the order path: reconciling the day's takings means reading every bill and changing none.
Open an order for a table, a takeaway or a delivery.

Add, change and send dishes, mark them served, split a bill, add packaging or an optional service charge, and cancel an order that was never settled. The server recomputes every price and tax from the menu; the client sends only what was ordered.

Take payment and settle a bill, which numbers the invoice, posts the stock the dishes consumed and freezes their food cost. Held by a waiter, because the person at the table is the person who takes the money.

Cancel an invoice on its day of issue, or issue a credit note and refund against a settled bill. Not held by a waiter: cancelling a paid cash bill is how the cash disappears, so it needs a more senior person and a reason, and a cancelled invoice keeps its number.
Apply a discount or a comp, always with a reason and always with this person's name on it. Not held by a waiter: the P1 design names discounts one of the classic leakage vectors.
Open and close the till, count the cash, and record payouts and post-close adjustments. Added to the P1 design by the M07 spec: a waiter takes cash and never closes the till that cash went into.

Switch busy mode on or off for the floor, so a settled table is free at once instead of being cleared first. It switches itself off at the next business day. Held by owner and manager: it changes how the whole floor behaves, not one table.

Choose who serves a table when opening an order for someone else, and move an order from one waiter to another with a reason. Held by owner and manager: a waiter may claim an order nobody is serving, but taking a table somebody is serving would take its credit, which M17 turns into a performance score.

See the kitchen display: what each station has to cook, how long each ticket has been waiting, and which are late. A waiter holds this and not kot.update, which is the design's own line - the floor watches the kitchen and does not drive it.

Move a ticket through the kitchen - acknowledge it, start it, mark it ready - and ask for a remake with a reason. It never marks anything served: a dish is served when it reaches a table, which the kitchen cannot see, so that is written from the order screen by whoever carried it.

Record something thrown away: what, how much and why. The cost is computed by the server from the batches the stock actually came out of and is never asked of the person logging - a cook does not know what a kilo of paneer cost on the day it was delivered, and asking would either get a guess or stop them logging at all. Held by the chef, the kitchen staff, the manager and the store manager; a waiter does not hold it.

Sign off waste logged against a reason the restaurant marked as needing approval - the expensive ones, such as expiry and quality rejection. It is the control standing between a reason code and somebody logging theft as waste, which is why the manager and the store manager hold it and the people who log most of the waste do not.

See a customer's profile: their number, how often they have been, what they usually order and how they like it. Held by a waiter as well as a manager, because greeting a regular by name and remembering they eat no onion is the whole point of keeping the record - asking a regular for the fourth time whether they eat onion is a small insult, and remembering is a small delight. A person sees the customers of the restaurant they are working in, not the whole organization's.

Create and edit a customer, record their preferences, capture or withdraw a consent, export everything held about them, and erase them at their request. Erasure destroys every detail that names a person and keeps every order, because a bill is a financial record; it cannot be undone, and afterwards the same person returning is a new customer with no history.

Read what diners said: the three questions from the QR code on the bill, per order and per day. Held by a waiter deliberately - a rating is about a table they served, and somebody who cannot see how their service landed cannot improve it. What nobody can do is submit feedback on their own tables: that needs the token printed on the guest's bill.

Log a complaint, give it an owner, and record what was actually done about it - a comp, a remake, a refund, an apology. A complaint nobody owns is worse than no system, which is why assigning is part of the same permission as logging. Whether the customer came back afterwards is not typed by anybody: it is derived from the order ledger, because it is the only honest measure of recovery and it becomes true weeks after everyone has forgotten.

Take part in the restaurant's conversations: read the threads you are in, post to them, and attach a photograph or a document. Held by every role, cleaner included, because the person who finds the broken freezer at 6am is exactly the person with no other permissions. It does not open every thread - you see a conversation because you are a participant in it, and being added to one is somebody's decision, not a permission.
See the work assigned to you, and write down work for yourself. Held by every role. Somebody without task.assign sees their own tasks and the ones they created, never the whole restaurant's board.

Give work to somebody else, move it to a different person, change what it says, cancel it, and verify that finished work was actually done. Giving a colleague a task is a manager's act, which is why it is separate from writing one down for yourself. Verifying your own completed work is refused unless you are the owner - the person who did the work is not the person who says it was done.

Move a task you were assigned along its lifecycle - accept it, start it, finish it. Held by every role, and the service refuses it on somebody else's task: nobody completes work on another person's behalf, because that is the one thing the record exists to prevent.

Read the roster and clock yourself in and out. Held by every role: a roster nobody can read is a noticeboard in a locked room. What it shows depends on who is asking - somebody without shift.manage sees their own shifts and who is covering which section right now, never the corrections or the whole week's statuses.

Create shifts, put people on them, set somebody absent or on leave, and correct a clock time. A correction always needs a reason and always writes an audit entry, because asserting somebody else's attendance is not the same act as their clocking in and the record must not make the two look alike.

Read the operational reports: what each dish sold and earned, where it sits on the menu, how long it took the kitchen, and what was thrown away. Held by a manager and a store manager as well as the owner, because these are the numbers somebody running a service can actually act on before the next one.

Read the money: revenue, covers, average bill, the payment split, and the food-cost variance that shows what was used against what the recipes say should have been. Held by the owner and the accountant. A manager is deliberately not given it - running the floor and reading the books are different jobs, and the design draws that line rather than showing a manager a screen full of blanks.

Read the audit trail: who changed a price, who voided a bill, who granted a role, and what the value was before and after. Held by the owner, the administrator and the accountant. A manager is deliberately not given it - the person who runs the floor is frequently the subject of the record, and a record its subject curates is not a record.

roles.name: Owner
roles.description: The person whose money is at risk. Holds everything, always.

roles.name: Administrator
roles.description: The owner's delegate for system configuration. Trusted, not operational.

roles.name: Manager
roles.description: Runs the floor. Staffs a shift at 7am when the owner is not on site, and appoints junior roles and other managers — but can never promote anyone above manager, nor change their own roles. Every assignment is written to the audit trail.

roles.name: Chef
roles.description: Runs the kitchen and needs to know who is on. Reads the staff list, changes nothing.

roles.name: Kitchen Staff
roles.description: Cooks to tickets. Nothing in M01.

roles.name: Waiter
roles.description: Takes orders and takes the money: holds order.settle and NOT order.void, order.discount or cash.manage, which are the classic leakage vectors. Staff records carry phone numbers and dates of birth, so no access there.

roles.name: Store Manager
roles.description: Runs the store room and supplier relationships. Manages stock, not people.

roles.name: Cleaner
roles.description: Referenced by tasks and shifts. Frequently has no login at all.

roles.name: Accountant
roles.description: Reads the staff list because payroll needs to know who is employed, and reconciles what suppliers billed against what arrived. Holds purchase.manage and NOT stock.receive: an accountant may raise an order and may never sign for a delivery. Reads every order and changes none: order.view is the whole of its order path.
